description: Break down monthly salary into basic pay, allowances and deductions. See the arithmetic clearly using your own figures, without sharing payroll details.
how: Enter basic salary, housing, transport, other allowances and deductions in one currency. Gross pay is the sum of earnings; estimated net pay subtracts deductions.
example: Basic 5,000 + housing 1,500 + transport 500 = gross 7,000. With deductions of 200, estimated net pay is 6,800.
mistakes: Do not enter an annual allowance as a monthly amount or count employer-paid housing twice.
limitations: This is an arithmetic breakdown, not a payroll, tax or social-insurance assessment.

faq.q: Does this calculate statutory deductions?
faq.a: No. Enter deductions already known from your contract or payroll.

faq.q: Can I use any currency?
faq.a: Yes, provided every amount uses the same currency and pay period.

description: Convert pay per period into annual salary and add known bonuses. Compare consistent figures using a transparent formula and your chosen payment frequency.
how: Multiply pay per period by the number of payments per year, then add annual bonuses separately.
example: Monthly pay of 6,000 paid 12 times gives 72,000 per year; a 3,000 annual bonus gives 75,000.
mistakes: Do not add a monthly bonus again as an annual bonus. Weekly and monthly pay need different multipliers.
limitations: Annualized pay assumes the supplied payment schedule continues for a full year.

faq.q: Is annual salary the same as take-home pay?
faq.a: Only if the periodic amount you enter is already net pay.

faq.q: Should I include an uncertain bonus?
faq.a: Keep guaranteed and uncertain bonuses separate when comparing offers.

description: Calculate a salary increase from your current pay and a proposed percentage. See the increase amount and revised salary with a simple, explainable formula.
how: Multiply current pay by the increase percentage divided by 100. Add that increase to current pay.
example: An 8% increase on 5,000 is 400, giving revised pay of 5,400.
mistakes: Use 8 for eight percent, not 0.08. Keep the same pay period before and after the raise.
limitations: The result excludes changes to tax, benefits and deductions.

faq.q: Does a raise increase every allowance?
faq.a: This tool applies the percentage only to the amount you enter.

faq.q: Can I calculate an increase on basic salary only?
faq.a: Yes. Enter basic salary rather than the total package.

description: Measure the percentage change between old and new salary. Distinguish the cash difference from the relative increase or decrease using comparable pay figures.
how: Subtract old salary from new salary, divide by old salary and multiply by 100. The baseline must be greater than zero.
mistakes: Do not divide by new salary; that answers a different question.
limitations: A zero baseline has no defined percentage change. Salary periods and currencies must match.

faq.q: Can the result be negative?
faq.a: Yes. A negative result means the new amount is lower than the old amount.

faq.q: Why is my cash increase not my percentage increase?
faq.a: The percentage expresses that cash difference relative to your original salary.

description: Compare two salaries on a consistent annual basis and subtract your own expenses. See why a larger headline salary may leave less money after living costs.
how: Normalize both salaries to annual pay. Compare annual earnings and the amount left after the expenses you supply.
example: Offer A pays 72,000 yearly with 36,000 expenses, leaving 36,000. Offer B pays 84,000 with 54,000 expenses, leaving 30,000.
mistakes: Avoid mixing gross salary with net salary or currencies without an explicit conversion.
limitations: No live salary benchmark, tax estimate or cost-of-living database is used.

faq.q: Does a higher salary always win?
faq.a: No. Compare expenses, benefits and personal priorities as well.

faq.q: Are expenses automatically filled for a city?
faq.a: No. Supply figures that reflect your own household.

description: Estimate the months needed to reach a savings goal using your savings and monthly contribution. See the calculation without investment-return assumptions.
how: Subtract saved funds from the goal and divide the remaining amount by monthly saving. Round up to whole months.
example: A 20,000 goal minus 5,000 saved leaves 15,000. Saving 2,000 monthly requires 8 months.
mistakes: Use money actually available for this goal, not emergency funds committed elsewhere.
limitations: Assumes fixed monthly contributions with no interest, inflation or withdrawals. Zero saving cannot reach an unmet goal.

faq.q: What if I already reached the goal?
faq.a: No additional saving months are needed.

faq.q: Does the final month need a full contribution?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Rounding up means the final contribution may be smaller.

description: Plan a monthly budget using your income and expense categories. Find the remaining balance and savings share with figures you control and clear assumptions.
how: Add monthly expenses, subtract their total from monthly income, and divide the remaining balance by income for the savings share.
example: Income of 8,000 minus expenses of 6,000 leaves 2,000, or 25% of income.
mistakes: Convert annual bills into monthly provisions and include irregular expenses.
limitations: A budget is a plan, not a bank balance or guarantee. Savings percentage is undefined with zero income.

faq.q: Can the balance be negative?
faq.a: Yes. A negative balance shows planned expenses exceed income.

faq.q: Should loan repayments be included?
faq.a: Include the monthly cash payment in an appropriate expense category.

description: Estimate a remittance with your own exchange rate and transfer fees. See the amount received without implying access to live rates or a transfer provider.
how: Subtract the sending fee in the sending currency, multiply by receiving-currency units per one sending unit, then subtract the receiving fee.
example: Send 1,000 with a 10 sending fee at 22 receiving units per sending unit: 990 × 22 = 21,780. A 50 receiving fee leaves 21,730.
mistakes: Do not reverse the exchange rate or enter the same fee in both currencies.
limitations: Rates and provider fee structures vary. This tool does not send money or fetch live quotes.

faq.q: Where do I find the rate?
faq.a: Use a current quote from the provider you intend to use.

faq.q: Is the sending fee added on top?
faq.a: This formula deducts it from the entered amount. If a provider charges it on top, adjust your input accordingly.

description: Compare living costs in two places using your own household expenses. Review category totals in a common currency without relying on generic city averages.
how: Enter corresponding expense categories for each location in the same currency and period. Sum each set and compare totals.
example: Monthly costs of 4,000 in A and 5,200 in B differ by 1,200; B is 30% higher relative to A.
mistakes: Use equivalent housing, household size and transport choices when comparing locations.
limitations: No city price database, live exchange rate or affordability guarantee is included.

faq.q: Can I compare different currencies?
faq.a: Convert them into one currency before entering the amounts.

faq.q: Does the result include school fees?
faq.a: Only when you include them in your supplied expenses.

description: Compare job offers using your own priorities for compensation and benefits. Inspect transparent weights instead of treating a single score as career advice.
how: Choose criteria, rate both offers on the same scale and set nonnegative weights. Divide the weighted total by total weight.
example: Salary rating 8 at weight 2 and work-life rating 6 at weight 1 gives (8 × 2 + 6 × 1) ÷ 3 = 7.33.
mistakes: A high weight magnifies a criterion. Do not compare ratings based on different scales.
limitations: Scores express your judgments, not objective employer quality or a recommendation to accept.

faq.q: Must all weights add to 100?
faq.a: No. Relative weights work when divided by their total; the total must be positive.

faq.q: Can I include relocation or family priorities?
faq.a: Yes. Use criteria that matter to your decision and rate them consistently.

description: Compare resume text with job-description keywords locally in your browser. Inspect matched and missing terms without sending your CV to an AI service.
how: Paste the resume and job description. The tool normalizes text, extracts distinct eligible job-description terms and checks which occur in the resume.
example: If eligible terms are inspection, calibration, safety and reporting, and three appear in the resume, overlap is 3 ÷ 4 = 75%.
mistakes: Do not add a missing skill unless it truthfully describes your experience.
limitations: Term overlap is a deterministic text check, not an employer ATS score or shortlisting probability.

faq.q: Does this understand equivalent phrases?
faq.a: Only the normalization rules shown by the tool; it does not infer all synonyms or meaning.

faq.q: Should I repeat keywords many times?
faq.a: No. Distinct-term matching does not reward unnecessary repetition.

description: Extract repeated words from a job description with a transparent text rule. Use the shortlist to review role language without inventing skills or requirements.
how: Paste the job description. Tokenization and a disclosed stopword filter remove common filler; remaining terms are ranked by occurrence.
example: A description containing calibration three times and commissioning twice ranks calibration above commissioning.
mistakes: Frequency alone does not establish importance. Read mandatory qualifications and context.
limitations: This is a word-frequency aid, not semantic analysis or a complete list of hiring requirements.

faq.q: Are every extracted word and skill the same thing?
faq.a: No. Some terms describe employers, locations or general duties.

faq.q: Can an important term occur only once?
faq.a: Yes. Review the original description as well as the ranked list.

description: Count resume words, characters and lines in pasted text. Review document length locally with a clear counting convention rather than a universal resume limit.
how: Paste text. Words are whitespace-separated tokens; character and line counts use the conventions stated beside the result.
example: The phrase “Led site commissioning” contains 3 whitespace-separated words.
mistakes: PDF layout and copied tables can introduce extra line breaks or merge words.
limitations: Counts do not assess writing quality or determine whether a recruiter will accept a resume.

faq.q: Is there one ideal resume word count?
faq.a: No. Appropriate length depends on experience, profession and application requirements.

faq.q: Why can Word show a different count?
faq.a: Applications may treat punctuation, hyphens and symbols differently.

description: Review resume bullet lengths against a threshold you choose. Find dense lines and inspect word counts without pretending there is one employer-approved limit.
how: Paste one bullet per line and set a word or character threshold. The checker marks lines exceeding that threshold.
example: With a 20-word threshold, a 24-word bullet is 4 words over your chosen limit.
mistakes: Do not remove useful evidence solely to hit a number. Wrapped text may need line-break cleanup.
limitations: The threshold is a writing preference, not a verified ATS rejection rule.

faq.q: Can a long bullet still be useful?
faq.a: Yes. Clarity and relevant evidence matter more than an arbitrary count.

faq.q: Does this rewrite bullets?
faq.a: No. It identifies length so you can edit truthfully.

description: Check whether resume bullets start with a listed action verb. Review weak openings locally using a visible vocabulary list and your professional judgment.
how: The checker reads each bullet opening and compares it with the displayed action-verb list.
example: “Led commissioning activities” starts with “Led”; “Responsible for commissioning” starts with “Responsible”.
mistakes: A strong verb does not justify invented achievements or exaggerated responsibility.
limitations: The curated list is incomplete. Unrecognized verbs are review prompts, not grammar errors.

faq.q: Does passing this check make a bullet strong?
faq.a: No. Specific, accurate context and outcomes still matter.

faq.q: Can I use present-tense verbs?
faq.a: Yes. Choose tense that matches current or completed work.

description: Review email, phone and LinkedIn contact formats before sharing a resume. Inspect syntax locally without claiming that an address, number or profile is real.
how: Enter the contact values. The tool checks their visible structure and flags malformed or incomplete entries.
example: A value such as name.example.com lacks an email @ separator and should be reviewed.
mistakes: Avoid accidental spaces, copied punctuation or a LinkedIn address belonging to another person.
limitations: Syntax checks do not verify email delivery, phone ownership, profile existence or identity.

faq.q: Does a valid format mean the email works?
faq.a: No. Confirm it through your own account or communication.

faq.q: Will this contact anyone?
faq.a: No. The format check does not send messages or make calls.

description: Check pasted resume text for section headings. Find possible omissions and review structure without assuming every profession needs identical sections.
how: Paste text. The checker searches for disclosed common headings and reports which were recognized.
example: A resume with “Experience”, “Education” and “Skills” recognizes those headings; a custom “Selected Work” title may need manual review.
mistakes: Do not add irrelevant sections just to clear every prompt.
limitations: Heading detection can miss unusual labels and cannot confirm that a section contains sufficient evidence.

faq.q: Is a professional summary mandatory?
faq.a: No. Decide whether it helps your application and follow employer instructions.

faq.q: Can custom sections be useful?
faq.a: Yes. Projects, portfolios and specialist work may be important for your profession.

description: Review employment date ranges for reversed dates and overlaps. Inspect possible inconsistencies while keeping concurrent jobs and ambiguous source text visible.
how: Enter explicit start and end dates for each role. The checker compares ordering and intersections without deciding whether overlap is an error.
example: A role ending 30 June and another starting 1 July has no overlap under inclusive date ranges.
mistakes: Do not treat concurrent part-time roles as automatically incorrect or guess missing months.
limitations: Ambiguous or incomplete dates need confirmation. The tool cannot verify employment history.

faq.q: Are overlapping dates always wrong?
faq.a: No. Concurrent roles, consulting and transitions can explain them.

faq.q: What should I do with an unknown date?
faq.a: Check your records and retain an honest approximation rather than inventing precision.

description: Review an ATS formatting checklist before submitting your resume. Work through practical document checks without receiving a misleading employer ATS score.
how: Inspect your own file and mark each checklist item after checking it. Completion reflects your selections only.
example: Completing 6 of 8 checklist items means 75% of this checklist is marked complete; it is not a hiring-system score.
mistakes: Do not mark a check complete merely because a preview looks attractive. Follow the vacancy’s file requirements.
limitations: The checklist does not run an employer parser, inspect every document element or predict screening results.

faq.q: Can this guarantee ATS compatibility?
faq.a: No. Employers use different systems and settings.

faq.q: Should I follow the employer’s instructions first?
faq.a: Yes. Their requested format and submission method take priority.

description: Check a resume file’s size locally against a limit you supply. See bytes, MB and MiB without uploading or reading your CV content on a remote service.
how: Choose a local file and enter the destination’s size limit. Compare its bytes using the displayed decimal or binary unit.
example: 1,000,000 bytes is 1 MB in decimal units and about 0.954 MiB in binary units.
mistakes: Check whether the application portal means MB or MiB and whether its limit includes attachments.
limitations: File size does not establish file safety, readability, format validity or ATS compatibility.

faq.q: Is the file uploaded?
faq.a: No. The checker reads local file metadata.

faq.q: Does a smaller PDF always mean better quality?
faq.a: No. Compression can reduce readability; inspect the final document.

description: Calculate professional experience from multiple employment periods. Merge overlapping dates to avoid double counting time and see the date conventions used.
how: Enter explicit periods. Sort them, merge intersecting periods and total unique calendar days within the supplied range.
example: 1–10 January and 5–15 January cover 15 unique days when both endpoints count, not 21 days.
mistakes: Do not add concurrent jobs as if they happened consecutively.
limitations: Calendar duration does not convert part-time work into full-time equivalent experience or verify professional eligibility.

faq.q: Can I include internships?
faq.a: Include them if relevant, but label them honestly when reporting experience.

faq.q: Why is this different from adding each job duration?
faq.a: Overlapping days count once in total unique experience.

description: Find uncovered periods between employment dates. Review calendar gaps without assuming that study, care responsibilities or a career break is a negative.
how: Enter dated employment intervals. Merge overlaps and calculate the uncovered periods between adjacent intervals.
example: A role ending 31 January and the next beginning 1 March leaves February uncovered; in a non-leap year that is 28 days.
mistakes: Do not label a gap as unemployment without considering study, freelance work or other activities.
limitations: The result finds calendar gaps only and cannot explain their cause.

faq.q: Does this assess whether a gap is acceptable?
faq.a: No. Hiring context varies; prepare an accurate explanation where relevant.

faq.q: Are dates before my first job counted?
faq.a: Only if the tool explicitly asks you to define an analysis window.

description: Calculate time remaining before an interview using an date and time zone. Reduce scheduling confusion and keep the original invitation as your reference.
how: Enter the interview date, time and specified zone. Compare that instant with the current instant to show the remaining duration.
example: An interview 48 hours from the current instant has a two-day countdown regardless of the viewer’s display zone.
mistakes: Do not assume a recruiter’s local time is your own; confirm the invitation’s zone.
limitations: A countdown is not a reminder or calendar invitation. Device clock errors affect the result.

faq.q: Will I receive an alert?
faq.a: No. Add a separate calendar reminder if needed.

faq.q: What if the interview time has passed?
faq.a: The tool should show that the supplied instant is in the past rather than a negative future countdown.

description: Build an interview preparation checklist and track completed tasks. Adapt it to your role, then print a practical preparation list for your next interview.
how: Review suggested preparation tasks, add your own and mark completed items. Completion is completed tasks divided by total tasks.
example: If 3 of 5 tasks are complete, checklist progress is 60%.
mistakes: Do not confuse checklist completion with interview readiness or a predicted performance score.
limitations: Suggested tasks are general preparation prompts, not role-specific technical coaching.

faq.q: Can I add technical revision tasks?
faq.a: Yes. Add topics relevant to your actual role and interview.

faq.q: Is progress a readiness score?
faq.a: No. It measures completion of this list only.

description: Organize job applications in your browser with statuses and follow-up notes. Export a backup because local data can disappear when browser storage is cleared.
how: Add employer, role, application date and status. Update progress and export a backup before changing browsers or devices.
example: An application can move from Applied to Interview after an invitation; this is a status you set, not a recruiter update.
mistakes: Do not rely on one browser as your only record or store passwords and sensitive identity documents.
limitations: Records stay in this browser and may be lost when storage is cleared. There is no cross-device account sync.

faq.q: Does it apply for jobs?
faq.a: No. It records applications you manage yourself.

faq.q: Will the tracker follow me to another phone?
faq.a: Not automatically. Export and import a supported backup where available.

description: Build job-search links from your role and location keywords. Open searches on supported websites without scraping vacancies or claiming to submit applications.
how: Enter role and location. The tool URL-encodes your query and constructs a search link for the chosen supported site.
example: A role containing “Instrumentation & Control” must encode the ampersand so it remains part of the query.
mistakes: Use specific role terms and verify filters on the destination site.
limitations: Job-site URLs and search behavior can change. Results, login requirements and availability belong to the destination.

faq.q: Does the builder collect job listings?
faq.a: No. It creates links to external searches.

faq.q: Will it apply automatically?
faq.a: No. You review opportunities and apply on the destination site.

description: Count the characters in a LinkedIn headline against a limit you set. Review concise wording without claiming to verify LinkedIn’s current account rules.
how: Paste your headline and set the character limit you want to check. Count Unicode characters using the displayed convention.
example: A 120-character headline checked against a 150-character target leaves 30 characters.
mistakes: Emojis and combined characters may be counted differently by the destination application.
limitations: The target is user-selected and platform rules can change. Confirm acceptance in LinkedIn itself.

faq.q: Does a shorter headline rank higher?
faq.a: This tool makes no ranking claim. Clear, relevant wording matters.

faq.q: Does this update LinkedIn?
faq.a: No. Copy the text and update your profile yourself.

description: Draft a resignation letter using your own employer, role and proposed final date. Review the wording and contractual requirements before sending it yourself.
how: Enter the requested factual details. The template inserts them into a concise resignation letter for your review.
example: For a proposed final day of 30 June, the draft can state that date without deciding whether the required notice has been satisfied.
mistakes: Check names, dates, notice provisions and the correct recipient before sending.
limitations: A template does not establish valid notice, release from duties or legal compliance.

faq.q: Is the letter sent automatically?
faq.a: No. Review and send it through the appropriate channel yourself.

faq.q: Does it calculate my last working day?
faq.a: No. Supply a date you have checked against your circumstances.

description: Create an experience-letter draft using employment details. Prepare text for employer review without implying that the platform certifies your work history.
how: Provide name, employer, role, start/end dates and accurate duties. Generate a draft for an authorized employer representative to review.
example: A supplied role of Instrument Technician stays Instrument Technician; the template must not upgrade it to Engineer.
mistakes: Do not add unverified achievements, salary, signatures, company seals or endorsement claims.
limitations: The draft is not an issued certificate, employer verification or proof of employment.

faq.q: Can I use it as an official certificate immediately?
faq.a: No. The employer must review and issue any official letter through its process.

faq.q: Will duties be invented?
faq.a: No. Include only duties you supply and can support.

description: Draft a salary negotiation email from your offer, target and truthful reasons. Review a clear request without inventing market evidence or competing offers.
how: Enter the role, current offer, requested amount and supporting facts. The template presents a courteous request and leaves the decision to the employer.
example: An offer of 8,000 and target of 9,000 can be stated as a request for 9,000; it is not proof that 9,000 is market pay.
mistakes: Do not invent another offer, salary benchmark or achievement to justify the request.
limitations: The template does not predict negotiation success or assess local compensation markets.

faq.q: Will it send the email?
faq.a: No. Review the draft and send it yourself.

faq.q: Can I negotiate benefits instead?
faq.a: Yes. Supply an accurate request for relevant benefits rather than an unsupported cash claim.

description: Count working days between dates using your chosen weekends and holidays. See an inclusive calculation without assuming every country follows the same calendar.
how: Count both endpoints, remove selected weekend days, then remove supplied holidays that would otherwise be working days.
example: 1–7 June 2026 contains 7 days. With Saturday/Sunday weekends it has 5 working days; a Monday holiday reduces it to 4.
mistakes: Do not subtract holidays twice when they already fall on a weekend.
limitations: No official public-holiday calendar is automatically supplied; working schedules vary.

faq.q: Can I choose Friday and Saturday as weekends?
faq.a: Yes. Select the days matching the schedule you need.

faq.q: Are start and end dates included?
faq.a: Yes, under this tool’s stated inclusive convention.

description: Find the calendar-day difference between two dates with a clear endpoint rule. Avoid daylight-saving surprises when comparing date-only career milestones.
how: Convert valid date-only inputs into UTC calendar dates and subtract them. The ordinary difference excludes the starting date.
example: 1 June to 2 June differs by 1 day; counting both dates inclusively would instead give 2 dates.
mistakes: Do not mix an elapsed-day difference with an inclusive count of dates.
limitations: Date-only arithmetic does not measure business days, hours worked or legal deadlines.

faq.q: Are weekends included?
faq.a: Yes. Use the Working Days Calculator to exclude them.

faq.q: Does the time zone change the answer?
faq.a: Not for validated date-only UTC calendar arithmetic.

description: Calculate completed age on a reference date using your date of birth. Review the date convention clearly without treating the result as an eligibility decision.
how: Enter a birth date and an on-date. Count completed anniversaries and the remaining calendar period under the displayed leap-day policy.
example: A person born 10 May 1990 is 36 completed years old on 10 May 2026.
mistakes: Check day/month order and do not use a future birth date.
limitations: Leap-day anniversary conventions vary. This tool does not determine immigration, pension or employment eligibility.

faq.q: Can I calculate age on a future date?
faq.a: Yes. Supply that reference date explicitly.

faq.q: What about 29 February birthdays?
faq.a: Use the policy displayed by the calculator; verify the relevant authority’s convention for legal use.

description: Calculate a percentage of an amount with visible arithmetic. Keep percentage values, proportions and percentage changes distinct when reviewing salary figures.
how: For a percentage of a value, multiply the value by the percentage and divide by 100. Other percentage questions require their own stated denominator.
mistakes: Enter 15 for fifteen percent and do not confuse a 15% increase with adding 15 currency units.
limitations: A percentage alone has no currency or pay-period meaning; interpret it with your inputs.

faq.q: Can percentages exceed 100?
faq.a: Yes in suitable contexts, provided the tool permits the relevant input.

faq.q: Is percentage change the same calculation?
faq.a: No. Change compares a difference with an original baseline.

description: Compare time-zone offsets at a specific instant, including seasonal clock changes where supported. Check interview scheduling with explicit zones and dates.
how: Choose two named zones and a reference instant. Obtain their UTC offsets at that instant and subtract the offsets.
example: Riyadh is UTC+03:00 and Kolkata UTC+05:30, so Kolkata is 2 hours 30 minutes ahead at an instant using those offsets.
mistakes: Do not reuse a winter offset for a summer meeting in a zone with seasonal changes.
limitations: Results depend on the browser’s time-zone data. Confirm important meetings against the invitation.

faq.q: Is the difference always a whole hour?
faq.a: No. Some zones use half-hour or quarter-hour offsets.

faq.q: Can the difference change during the year?
faq.a: Yes. Seasonal clock changes can alter it.

description: Count calendar days until a contract date you supply. Plan a review or renewal discussion without assuming that the contract automatically ends or renews.
how: Enter the contractual end date and the reference date. Show their calendar-day difference and clearly identify past dates.
example: From 1 June to 30 June the date difference is 29 days; an inclusive count of both dates is 30.
mistakes: Do not confuse a countdown with a required notice deadline or last day of attendance.
limitations: The date alone does not determine termination, renewal, notice or legal rights.

faq.q: Does the tool renew my contract?
faq.a: No. It displays a date-based countdown.

faq.q: Should I use it for legal notice?
faq.a: Check your contract and applicable rules separately; the countdown does not establish notice requirements.

description: Add a probation duration you supply to an employment start date. Inspect the date convention without relying on an assumed legal maximum or contract rule.
how: Enter the start date and calendar-day duration. Apply the stated inclusive or elapsed-day convention consistently.
example: For a start of 1 June and 30 counted calendar days, an inclusive final day is 30 June; adding 30 elapsed days gives 1 July.
mistakes: Do not mix calendar days with working days or ignore documented exclusions and extensions.
limitations: The tool does not establish a lawful probation length or whether exclusions apply.

faq.q: Is the entered duration legally allowed?
faq.a: The date calculation does not decide that. Check the applicable contract and law.

faq.q: Can unpaid absence extend probation?
faq.a: That depends on the applicable rules and contract; do not assume an extension from this arithmetic.

description: Plan annual leave using your selected dates, weekends, holidays and balance. Estimate days used without assuming an employer’s leave-accounting policy.
how: Count dates inclusively, remove selected nonworking days and supplied holidays, then subtract planned leave from the balance you enter.
example: A Monday–Friday period with no holidays uses 5 working days. A balance of 18 then leaves 13.
mistakes: Confirm whether your employer charges working days or calendar days and whether travel days count.
limitations: This planner does not establish entitlement, approval, carry-over or official holiday dates.

faq.q: Does it submit leave to my employer?
faq.a: No. Use your employer’s approval process.

faq.q: Can I use it for a calendar-day leave policy?
faq.a: Only use a configuration that matches that policy; do not automatically exclude weekends.

description: Create a printable checklist for applications, interviews or career tasks. Edit items, mark progress and use a clean print layout without creating an account.
how: Add a title and one task per item. Mark completed items, then review the print preview before printing or saving as PDF.
example: A list with 2 completed tasks out of 4 shows 50% list completion.
mistakes: Avoid putting confidential identifiers or credentials on a checklist you intend to share.
limitations: Print layout and PDF options depend on your browser and device. Completion is not an assessment of task quality.

faq.q: Can I customize every item?
faq.a: Yes. Use tasks that fit your own workflow.

faq.q: Does printing save an online copy?
faq.a: No. Keep any file or paper copy you create yourself.

description: Turn structured career notes or a checklist into a printable document. Use your browser’s Save as PDF option and review the output before sharing it.
how: Enter a document title, section headings and notes or checklist items. Open print preview and choose Save as PDF if your browser offers it.
example: A title, an Interview preparation section and three tasks produce a structured document you can inspect in print preview.
mistakes: Review page breaks, paper size and whether browser headers or footers should be included.
limitations: This uses the browser’s print system. It does not promise identical pagination or a direct PDF download on every device.

faq.q: Is this a resume design or ATS certification tool?
faq.a: No. It exports your own structured notes or checklist.

faq.q: Where is the PDF stored?
faq.a: You choose a location through your device’s print or save dialog.
